translation.text: And they took me into a place where those who were there were like burning fire, and whenever they wished, they appeared like men.[a]

footnotes.text: Or 'they showed themselves like men.' The verb can carry the sense of making themselves visible in human form.

translation.text: And they took me to a place of whirlwind[b][a], and to a mountain whose summit reached to heaven.

footnotes.text: Or 'a place of storm' or 'a place of tempest.' The Ge'ez term conveys violent atmospheric turmoil.
Or 'into a place of whirlwind, and into a mountain'.

translation.text: And I saw the places of the lights and of the thunder, in the extremities, in the depth,[a] where there was a bow of fire, and arrows and their quivers, and a sword of fire,[b] and all the lightnings.

footnotes.text: Not ready for application: the selected starred extremity/depth construction is difficult, and the exact starred noun ending remains glyph-provisional in this author proposal. The literal extremities and depth wording is not a silently reconstructed airy depth or a claim about a mapped earthly site. Charles discusses possible corruption in printed page 46 note 29; no proposed Greek-assisted replacement is adopted here.
The sequence 'bow ... arrows ... their quiver ... sword of fire' is preserved as weapon imagery in the vision, not paraphrased into a general storm description.

translation.text: And they took me as far as the living waters[a], and as far as the fire of the west, which receives every setting of the sun.

footnotes.text: Living waters follows the reading selected in the Charles 1906 edited Ethiopic body, ሕያዋን, rather than silently normalizing it to waters of life. Printed page 46 note 37 says this living form follows a reported superscription and the Greek; the printed edited Greek has ὑδάτων ζώντων. This is an editorial/reported-reading dependency, not fresh manuscript inspection. The following [ዘይትናገር፡], which speaks, remains bracketed in the source and is not represented in the narrative English: printed note 38 calls it an Ethiopic gloss. No physical location or additional speaking agent is supplied.

translation.text: And I came to a river of fire, whose fire flowed like water, and it emptied into the great sea toward the west.[a]

footnotes.text: The final phrase literally reads something like 'in the direction of ʿarab.' It is rendered 'toward the west' because the expression can denote the western quarter, though some may understand a geographic reference such as Arabia.

translation.text: And I saw great rivers, and I reached as far as the great darkness, and I went to where no flesh walks.[a][b]

footnotes.text: Not ready for application: Charles inserts the parenthesized negative in accordance with the Greek, as printed page 47 note 48 states; the printed edited Greek has οὐ before the walking verb. No flesh walks therefore depends on this explicit editorial negative, not an unqualified claim of Ethiopic manuscript agreement. The exact vowel of the parenthesized Ethiopic glyph remains held for further font review; the source field is provisional there, and the old positive alternative is not adopted.
'All flesh' is a traditional Semitic expression that may refer to humankind broadly or to living creatures more generally.

translation.text: And I saw the mountains of winter darkness[a] and the outpouring of water from the whole deep[b].

footnotes.text: The selected noun ቀበሬት is supported in the actual primary Dillmann 1865 lexicon, column 436, in the darkness/obscurity range with an explicit Enoch 17:7 citation. Winter darkness renders that noun with the following winter expression; it does not substitute the different winds wording of the printed Greek comparison or identify a modern mountain range.
Or “outflow”; the source depicts the waters pouring out. The whole/all expression modifies the deep in the selected construction, not a silently moved all before the waters.

translation.text: And I saw the mouth[b] of all the earth’s rivers and the mouth of the deep[a].

footnotes.text: The Geʿez repeats “mouth” for the rivers and the deep; it does not specify whether these are sources or outlets.

The selected Geʿez has a singular mouth expression with a plural possessor for all the rivers. The English retains that collective singular rather than silently turning it into plural mouths or adding a separate mouth of the earth from the edited Greek comparison. It does not determine whether the visionary opening is a source or an outlet.
